author: Our World in Data
body:
The Internet remains one of the world’s fastest-growing technologies.

In 2010, just 28% of the global population was online. Within a decade, this figure had doubled to 60%. And it’s still growing rapidly, as the chart shows.

There are, however, large inequalities. In North America and Europe, more than 90% are online, compared to just 36% in Sub-Saharan Africa.

The quality of this access is also very different: this indicator is based on someone having used the Internet at least once in the last three months. The experience of someone with nonstop connections on their smartphone will be very different from that of someone logging on in a public space once a month.

But the dominant trend globally — and across all regions — is that more people are coming online every year. It’s a technology that’s moving incredibly fast.

(written by Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada)

Explore this data for 213 countries, by world region, or by income group: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/share-of-individuals-using-the-internet?tab=line

author: Our World in Data
body:
Most of the advanced economies of the world have been deindustrializing for decades and have moved into a new “post-industrial” phase of development. Although trends vary from country to country, the evidence shows that as rich countries developed, the relative contribution of agriculture to both total employment and GDP declined, while the contribution of services rose in both respects. In the middle, the relative importance of the manufacturing sector first expanded and then contracted. There was first a period of industrialization as production shifted from agriculture to manufacturing, followed by a period of deindustrialization as production shifted from manufacturing to services. This transition is a process of “structural transformation”.

A falling share of agriculture in GDP and employment does not necessarily mean that agricultural output falls in absolute terms. In Sweden, for example, despite the process of industrialization, agricultural output increased up to 1931, after which it fell slightly but then stabilized for many decades. Given that the share of agriculture in Sweden’s total employment was decreasing over this time, labor productivity in agriculture was actually growing.

The story of structural transformation is not one of a stagnant agricultural sector overtaken by dynamic manufacturing and service sectors; instead, what matters are the differences in productivity growth between sectors. “Deindustrialization” means a loss in the relative importance of the manufacturing sector. In absolute terms, industrial output might well go up as a country “deindustrializes”, just as agricultural output might go up during periods of “industrialization”.

Read our article: https://ourworldindata.org/structural-transformation-and-deindustrialization-evidence-from-todays-rich-countries

author: Our World in Data
body:
Globally, women are now more likely to enroll in higher education than men.

In the 1970s, outside of rich countries, very few people went on to higher education. Globally, it was more likely for men, but still uncommon.

The chart shows how this changed in the decades that followed: enrollment increased for both genders, but faster for women. The gap reversed at the turn of the century, and has widened since.

Today, two generations later, the global rates are 47% for women and 41% for men.

Both the expansion of higher education and the reversal of the gender gap have happened across most of the world. With the exception of Sub-Saharan Africa, the rate for women is now at least as high as the rate for men in all regions.

(written by Esteban Ortiz-Ospina)

Explore the data country by country in our interactive chart: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/school-enrolment?uniformYAxis=0&country=~OWID_WRL&tableFilter=all&tableSearch=latin&enrolment_type=gross_enrolment&level=tertiary&sex=sex_side_by_side

author: Our World in Data
body:
Look at a global map of deforestation, and you’ll notice a clear pattern. Most deforestation today is happening in the tropics, while much of the temperate world is gaining forest.

But it would be wrong to think that consumers in temperate countries don’t contribute to deforestation at all. They do, through the products they import from other parts of the world.

To understand the scale and sources of deforestation driven by traded foods, we’ve built a visualization that maps flows of deforestation risk from food trade. It maps deforestation flows from the country of origin — where it’s happening — to where the products grown are consumed.

We see a range of patterns across the world. In Brazil, for example, most deforestation occurs to meet domestic demand. Many high-income countries have very low domestic deforestation, but contribute far more through the goods they import.

You can explore this data for most countries and see how this traded deforestation has changed over the last two decades.

(This visualization was created by Hannah Ritchie, Pablo Rosado, and Marcel Gerber.)

Explore the data for your country: https://ourworldindata.org/how-much-deforestation-is-caused-by-the-products-we-produce-and-consume

author: Our World in Data
body:
Global electricity generation had tripled since 1985, and most of this growth had come from Asia. But the per-person picture is even more striking.

Look at Asia versus the rest of the world on the chart. Asia’s demand per person has almost tripled since 2000. In the rest of the world (excluding Asia), it’s fallen by around 11%. The two lines have converged.

Within world regions, trends differ. Demand per person in North America has fallen; barely changed in Europe and Africa; and increased by around 50% in South America. These mostly cancel out to average little change at all.

(written by Hannah Ritchie)

Explore how electricity generation and sources have changed across the world: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/electricity-mix

Other sources & data:

https://ourworldindata.org/data-insights/global-electricity-generation-has-tripled-since-1985-most-of-this-growth-came-from-asia

author: Our World in Data
body:
We have updated our topic page on mental health!

Mental health is an essential part of people’s lives. Poor mental health affects someone’s well-being, ability to work, and their relationships with friends, family, and community.

Mental health conditions are not uncommon. Every year, hundreds of millions of people experience them, and lifetime prevalence is even higher. It’s estimated that around half of us will experience a mental health disorder at some point in our lives.

But these conditions are treatable, and there are ways to reduce their severity and impact. Despite this, treatment is often lacking or of poor quality, and many feel uncomfortable sharing their symptoms with healthcare professionals or people they know.

To support them, it’s essential to have reliable data to understand these conditions — how, when, and why they occur, how many people are affected, and how they can be treated effectively and safely.

On this new version of our topic page, we show data on the prevalence of mental illnesses, their burden, treatments against them, and people’s attitudes toward mental health.

(This topic update was led by Hannah Ritchie.)

Read our new topic page: https://ourworldindata.org/mental-health

author: Our World in Data
body:
The United States Geological Survey (USGS) publishes its yearly Mineral Commodity Summaries, with production and reserves data for a wide range of minerals. We combine it with the World Mineral Statistics of the British Geological Survey (BGS). Together, they cover many of the minerals that batteries, solar panels, and electric cars need, with data up to 2025.

The combined data covers more than 150 countries, with world totals for some minerals going back to 1900 and country data for many from the 1970s. We recently updated hundreds of our charts with the latest release.

This chart tracks lithium mining each year. Global lithium mining reached an estimated 290,000 tonnes in 2025, about 30% more than in 2024 and around 20 times its 2000 level. In 2025, Australia was the biggest producer with an estimated 92,000 tonnes; China and Chile came next.

(This data update was led by Pablo Rosado.)

Explore all of the updated data in our interactive charts: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/minerals
